title: Proclamation of the German Empire: Berlin as Imperial Capital
shortDesc: The proclamation of the German Empire under Prussian leadership in January 1871 elevated Berlin from a provincial royal seat to the capital of a unified continental power (Clark, 2006). The ensuing influx of imperial institutions, capital, and migrants initiated the Gründerzeit building boom that produced the dense tenement fabric — the Mietskaserne — still characteristic of the city's inner districts.

title: Abdication of the Kaiser and the Weimar Republic
shortDesc: The abdication of Wilhelm II on 9 November 1918 and the simultaneous proclamation of a republic transformed Berlin into the contested political stage of Germany's first democracy (Weitz, 2007). Despite chronic instability, the Weimar years established Berlin as a laboratory of architectural and social modernism, from large-scale housing estates to an internationally influential cultural avant-garde.

title: National Socialist Seizure of Power
shortDesc: Hitler's appointment as Chancellor on 30 January 1933 initiated the rapid dismantling of the Weimar constitutional order and the coordination of state and society under National Socialist rule (Evans, 2003). In Berlin the regime pursued megalomaniac replanning under Albert Speer's 'Germania' scheme while persecuting the city's Jewish population, whose economic and cultural presence had been integral to its metropolitan character.

title: The Fall of Berlin
shortDesc: The Soviet capture of Berlin on 2 May 1945 concluded a battle that, together with years of aerial bombardment, left roughly a third of the city's building stock destroyed and much of the remainder damaged (Beevor, 2002). The scale of wartime destruction created the tabula rasa conditions that shaped postwar reconstruction debates in both halves of the subsequently divided city.

title: Construction of the Berlin Wall
shortDesc: On 13 August 1961 the German Democratic Republic sealed the sector boundary and erected a fortified barrier through the urban core, severing streets, rail lines, and neighbourhoods (Harrison, 2003). The Wall froze the city's development along an artificial axis for twenty-eight years, producing duplicate infrastructures on either side and a depopulated death strip whose reintegration would dominate post-1990 planning.

title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
shortDesc: The unplanned opening of the border crossings on 9 November 1989 — the product of bureaucratic miscommunication amid mounting popular pressure — ended the physical division of the city (Sarotte, 2014). The event triggered an immediate reconnection of severed urban networks and released the central death-strip corridor for what became one of Europe's largest inner-city redevelopment programmes.

title: German Reunification
shortDesc: The accession of the German Democratic Republic to the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990 restored Berlin's formal status as capital of a unified Germany (Jarausch, 1994). Reunification confronted the city with the unprecedented task of merging two administrative systems, two housing markets, and two incompatible infrastructure networks within a single municipality.

title: The Bundestag Returns to the Reichstag
shortDesc: The German parliament's move from Bonn into Norman Foster's reconstructed Reichstag in April 1999 completed the governmental relocation mandated by the 1991 capital decision (Wise, 1998). The building's glass cupola, publicly accessible above the plenary chamber, was conceived as an architectural statement of democratic transparency and became the emblem of the 'Berlin Republic'.

title: FIFA World Cup: Berlin on the Global Stage
shortDesc: Berlin hosted the final of the 2006 FIFA World Cup in the refurbished Olympiastadion, an event widely credited with projecting an image of an open, post-unification Germany to international audiences (Kersting, 2007). The tournament accelerated investment in transport and public space and marked the city's consolidation as a global tourism destination.
